stories.title: Shorter Stays Ahead: Thailand Cuts Visa-Free Time for Singaporeans
stories.headline_kid: From 15 September, Singaporeans visiting Thailand without a visa can only stay for 30 days instead of 60.
summary: Many Singaporean families love holidaying in Thailand — think Bangkok's street food, Phuket's beaches or Chiang Mai's mountains. Right now, Singaporeans can visit Thailand without needing a visa and stay for up to 60 days.
But starting 15 September, that visa-free stay will be cut in half to just 30 days. This new rule applies not only to Singapore, but to dozens of other countries too.

Thai officials say the change is meant to reduce crime linked to foreigners who overstay or misuse their long visa-free periods. Tourism is very important to Thailand's economy, so officials are trying to balance welcoming visitors with keeping the country safe.

For most families, this won't change much, since typical holidays last only a week or two. But anyone planning a longer trip — like working remotely from Thailand or visiting relatives for a long school break — will need to check the new rules carefully.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a long holiday in Thailand, you might need to check how many days you're allowed to stay.
lenses.family: Parents booking trips during the year-end school holidays should double-check visa rules before flying.
lenses.friends: Classmates who visit relatives in Thailand during long breaks may be affected if their trips are longer than 30 days.
lenses.nation: Singapore has close travel and trade ties with Thailand, so changes like this affect how easily Singaporeans can visit.
lenses.world: It shows how countries are tightening travel rules to manage safety and crime linked to foreign visitors.

stories.title: Good News: Fewer Teen Mums in Singapore Than Ever Before
stories.headline_kid: Only 140 babies were born to teenage mums in Singapore last year — the lowest number in more than 20 years!
summary: In 2025, only 140 babies were born to teenage mothers in Singapore. That's a huge drop of more than 40% from 244 births the year before, and it's the lowest number in over two decades.

A 'teen birth' means a baby born to a mother who is still a teenager, usually under 20 years old. Experts say this drop is a good sign that young people are learning more about making safe and healthy choices as they grow up.

One big reason for the change, experts say, is that more teenagers now feel comfortable asking for help without being judged. Having a safe, non-judgmental place to ask questions — whether from parents, teachers or health professionals — makes a real difference.
This story reminds us that talking openly about health, without embarrassment or fear, helps young people stay safe and make better decisions for their future.

lenses.me: It shows that learning about health and making safe choices in school really can help protect young people.
lenses.family: Families who talk openly and calmly about growing up help their children feel safe asking questions.
lenses.friends: Friends can look out for each other and share where to find trustworthy help if someone is worried about something.
lenses.nation: It reflects Singapore's efforts to improve health education and support services for young people.
lenses.world: Many countries around the world are also seeing teen birth rates fall as health education and support improve.

stories.title: Nepal Flood: Deaths Pass 1,000, Rescuers Search Tunnels for Survivors
stories.headline_kid: More than a week after a giant flood of mud and water hit Nepal's mountains, over 1,000 people have died, and rescuers are now searching underground tunnels for survivors.
summary: About a week ago, a huge chunk of glacier ice collapsed high in the Himalayan mountains, sending a massive wave of water, rocks and mud crashing down onto villages in Nepal. This week, the number of confirmed deaths passed 1,000, and nearly 4,500 people are still missing across Nepal and nearby Tibet.

Rescue teams are now focusing on hydropower project tunnels, where workers were on duty when the flood struck. A tunnel expert named Arnold Dix believes some workers may have sheltered in large underground spaces, giving rescuers hope of finding survivors even after so many days.

Because so many people are still missing, some Nepali families have held symbolic funerals — special ceremonies to say goodbye to loved ones they may never find. This is a way for families to find some peace, even without a body to bury.

Nepal's foreign minister called the disaster a 'warning signal' about how climate change is making mountain regions more dangerous. Singapore has sent teams, including specialist police and rescue officers, to help with search and relief efforts.

lenses.me: It's a reminder to feel grateful for safety and to think about how we can help others facing hardship.
lenses.family: Families in Singapore might consider donating to relief efforts to help Nepali families rebuild.
lenses.friends: It's a chance to talk with friends about kindness and supporting people affected by disasters far away.
lenses.nation: Singapore continues sending help to Nepal, showing how our country supports others during crises.
lenses.world: The disaster highlights how climate change is making natural disasters more frequent and severe worldwide.

stories.title: Indonesia Shuts 9 National Parks to Fight Forest Fires
stories.headline_kid: Indonesia has closed nine national parks and is fighting fires in six provinces — and the smoky haze could soon drift towards Singapore.
summary: Forest fires are burning in parts of Indonesia's Kalimantan and Sumatra islands, which are located near Singapore. To focus on putting out the flames, Indonesian authorities have temporarily closed nine national parks and are prioritising firefighting efforts in six provinces.

Some areas in Borneo (part of Kalimantan) are already blanketed in 'hazardous' haze — thick, smoky air that can make it hard to breathe and see clearly. Haze happens when smoke from burning forests and land spreads across the sky, sometimes travelling hundreds of kilometres.

Indonesia's Forestry Minister said the closures are meant to protect both the parks and firefighting teams while outbreaks of fire are brought under control. Dry weather in the region has made it easier for fires to spread quickly.

Singapore keeps a close watch on the haze situation, because winds can carry the smoke here too. When haze levels rise, Singaporeans are usually advised to limit outdoor activities and wear masks if needed.

lenses.me: If haze reaches Singapore, you might need to stay indoors more and check the air quality (PSI) before playing outside.
lenses.family: Families may need to postpone outdoor outings or picnics if the haze becomes bad.
lenses.friends: Schools may cancel outdoor sports or recess activities if the air quality turns unhealthy.
lenses.nation: Singapore monitors the haze closely and works with neighbouring countries to reduce its impact.
lenses.world: It shows how fires in one country can affect the health and daily life of people in nearby countries too.

stories.title: Football Frenzy: Premier League Clubs Smash Spending Record
stories.headline_kid: English Premier League clubs just spent more money than ever before to sign new football players this summer!
summary: The Premier League is one of the most popular football leagues in the world, and it's watched by huge numbers of fans in Singapore too, on channels like Singtel TV and StarHub. This summer, Premier League clubs broke the all-time record for how much money they spent buying and loaning players.

Some exciting moves happened during this 'transfer window' — a period when clubs can buy, sell or loan players. Ukrainian forward Mykhailo Mudryk joined Tottenham Hotspur on loan from Chelsea, while star player Jack Grealish returned to Everton on loan from Manchester City.
Clubs spend big money hoping talented players will help them win matches and trophies. But some fans and experts worry that such huge spending makes football feel more like a business than a sport.
For Singaporean football fans, this means new faces to watch when the new season kicks off — and plenty to talk about with friends over the next few months.

lenses.me: If you support Chelsea, Tottenham, Everton or Man City, these transfers change who you'll be cheering for this season.
lenses.family: Families who watch Premier League matches together on weekends now have new players and storylines to follow.
lenses.friends: Friends might have fun debates about which team made the smartest signings this summer.
lenses.nation: Singapore has a huge Premier League fan base, and matches are widely watched and discussed here.
lenses.world: It shows how football has become a massive global business, with clubs spending huge sums to compete for the best talent.

compo_words.example: Clubs spent an unprecedented amount of money this transfer window.
